info.bio: Band Aid era una unión Británica e Irlandesa de caridad en que participan grupos musicales. Ha sido fundada en 1984 por Bob Geldof y Midge Ure. El propósito era recaudar dinero para la familia de Etiopía y relanzando la canción "Do They Know It's Christmas?" El single fue todo un suceso. Fue número #1 en los charts musicales durante la Navidad. La canción fue regrabada dos veces. Ellos recaudaron más dinero y también terminó número #1 en los charts.

scenes.name: Segunda invasión británica y MTV
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En 1982 el new pop deja de ser un sueño de periodistas: «Don't You Want Me», «Tainted Love» y «The Look of Love» anuncian una nueva invasión, y en 1983 la segunda camada (Duran Duran, Culture Club, Wham!, Eurythmics, Thompson Twins) conquista Estados Unidos gracias a MTV, canal ideado por Michael Nesmith que, sin vídeos americanos, dependía de los británicos, más videogénicos y cultivados en el estilo («I want my MTV»). A Flock of Seagulls, Altered Images («Happy Birthday»), Simple Minds («Promised You a Miracle», New Gold Dream), Haircut 100, Kajagoogoo; Bowie se broncea con «Let's Dance». El new pop reexporta música negra (Chic, P-Funk, Quincy Jones) a la América blanca. En el Reino Unido, 1983 se vive en cambio como un año infausto: reelección de Thatcher, «Kill Ugly Pop» en las paredes y la vuelta de la conciencia social.

podcast.title: Recording "Do They Know It's Christmas?" (November 25, 1984)
podcast.body: Just two weeks after Bob Geldof saw the BBC documentary on the Ethiopian famine, 25 of Britain's most renowned musicians assembled at Sarm Studios in London's Notting Hill area on November 25, 1984. They gathered to record the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?", which marked the official beginning of the Band-Aid project. "On November the 25th, 1984, just two weeks after that BBC broadcast, 25 of Britain's most famous musicians gathered at Sarm studios in the Notting Hill area of London to crank out a song that was now called Do They Know It's Christmas?"

podcast.title: Initial Idea for a Benefit Record
podcast.body: The day after being deeply affected by the BBC documentary on the Ethiopian famine, Bob Geldof tentatively proposed the idea of a benefit record for Ethiopia at his record company's office. The suggestion was well-received by those present, setting the stage for the Band-Aid project. "he tentatively suggested that someone ought to put out a record for the Ethiopians. A benefit thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

podcast.title: Legacy and Impact of Band-Aid
podcast.body: The Band-Aid project, initiated by the "Do They Know It's Christmas?" single, generated significant funds for charity and inspired further philanthropic efforts in the music world. Its success led to the monumental Live Aid concerts the following July, as well as other charity singles from Canada and the US. More broadly, it fostered a renewed sense that rock and roll possessed a conscience and that music could genuinely effect positive change in the world. "The money raised by the band-aid single, the live-aid concerts the following July, the other charity singles from Canada and the US, and most of all the sense that Rock and Roll did have a conscience and that music could make a difference."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recruitment of Musicians for Band-Aid
podcast.body: Bob Geldof initiated the Band-Aid project by reaching out to prominent musicians to create a charity single. His first call was to Midge Ure of Ultravox, followed by Sting of The Police, and Simon Le Bon of Duran Duran. As word spread, other notable artists such as Bono, David Bowie, and Paul Weller of The Jam, enthusiastically joined the effort, forming a supergroup of British talent. "First, he called mid-Jour of the band UltraVox. Sting of the police was called next, and Simon LeBawn of Durand Iran, and as words spread more people jumped on board."

xref.title: Inspiration for Band-Aid (November 11, 1984)
xref.body: On the evening of November 11, 1984, after a difficult day attempting to publicize The Boomtown Rats' album "In the Long Grass," Bob Geldof watched a BBC documentary by reporter Michael Buerk detailing the famine in Ethiopia. Deeply affected by the images of starvation, Geldof felt compelled to take action, leading to the inception of the Band-Aid project. "Bob was stunned by the images of starving people, and he was suddenly moved to do something, anything to help these poor people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 3

xref.title: Bob Geldof's Self-Perception and Motivation
xref.body: As described in his autobiography, Bob Geldof felt his limited influence as a "not very successful pop singer" making records "that no one bought" underscored his initial dilemma in responding to the Ethiopian famine. This self-assessment, however, fueled his determination to find a way to make a difference, ultimately leading to the creation of Band-Aid. "As he wrote in his autobiography, I was only a pop singer, and by now not a very successful pop singer, all I could do was make records that no one bought."
